name_note: NCBI names these genomes Candidatus Lachnocurva; the literature calls the single known species Candidatus Lachnocurva vaginae, previously bacterial vaginosis-associated bacterium 1 (BVAB1).

sentences.text: Bacterial vaginosis-associated bacterium 1 (BVAB1) is an as-yet uncultured bacterial species found in the human vagina that belongs to the family Lachnospiraceae, renamed Candidatus Lachnocurva vaginae on phylogenetic grounds.
It was one of three unclassified species designated in 2005 that were highly preponderant in the vagina of females with bacterial vaginosis, and can be identified only through metagenomics.

The bacterium is often associated with bacterial vaginosis, a common vaginal disorder that has been shown to increase risk for HIV, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections and preterm birth.
It has been further associated with the persistence of bacterial vaginosis following metronidazole treatment, increased vaginal inflammation, and adverse obstetrics outcomes.
Genomic and metabolomic evidence suggests this candidate species may metabolize D-lactate, produce trimethylamine, one of the chemicals responsible for BV-associated odor, and be motile.
